title: Verifier‑Assisted vs. LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We evaluate whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier into a generative LLM pipeline increases the proportion of network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation. Following a preregistered paired design (study cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001), we generated 300 intent-driven configuration-change tasks stratified by complexity and executed, per pair, a single shared LLM generation under two conditions: (1) baseline (LLM-only single shot) and (2) guarded (LLM + verifier with up to one automated repair). Primary outcome was an unflagged verifier pass (semantic pass and no automated-flag). Using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) on a synthetic topology suite, 299/300 baseline episodes and 300/300 guarded episodes produced unflagged verifier passes. The absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap seed 1729). Confirmatory result: the preregistered primary hypothesis (a meaningful paired improvement of ≥10 percentage points) was not supported in this benchmark because baseline performance was already near‑ceiling. We report the preregistered design, complete execution artifacts, and deterministic analysis. We discuss implications for NetOps pipelines, failure modes, and next steps for benchmarking verifier utility under more challenging and diverse conditions.

sections.introduction: LLMs are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent-to-configuration translation, template synthesis, and repair. Prior work shows tool‑augmented architectures and generate→validate→repair patterns can reduce syntactic and some semantic errors, but open questions remain about the marginal operational benefit of adding verifiers when generation quality is high. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment to measure the incremental effect of a verifier in an LLM-driven pre‑deployment workflow. The research question was: does a verifier-assisted pipeline increase the fraction of change proposals that pass semantic pre‑deployment validation (unflagged) compared with a single-shot LLM generation? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation (N=300 pairs) using a shared-generation protocol; (2) a fully archived execution and analysis artifact bundle; (3) a measured outcome showing negligible paired improvement on a synthetic NetOps benchmark and a discussion of causes and implications.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and system papers document active research into LLMs for network configuration, intent translation, and tool-augmented agents (e.g., MeshAgent's constraint‑guided adaptation [10.1145/3771567], API-Bank and tool-use benchmarks [arXiv:2304.08244], planner-centric tool architectures [10.1609/aaai.v40i40.40676], and NeTestLLM for protocol testing [arXiv:2510.13248]). Empirical and design reports show that validators or syntactic/semantic checkers improve correctness relative to unconstrained generation in many settings; however, reported improvements are task- and dataset-dependent. Work on hallucination detection and deterministic safety nets highlights epistemic risks that motivate verifier integration (e.g., entropy- and retrieval-based detectors). Our study contributes a preregistered, execution‑level comparison that isolates the verifier's incremental effect in a controlled synthetic NetOps suite.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered (cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) and frozen before observing outcomes. Design: paired confirmatory experiment with N=300 independent intent pairs (100 per complexity stratum: low/medium/high). For each pair the pipeline produced one shared initial LLM generation (shared_initial) and then applied two condition treatments deterministically: baseline = accept the shared_initial as the baseline episode; guarded = run the verifier on the shared_initial and apply at most one automated repair call if the verifier failed, then revalidate. The primary estimand was the paired absolute difference in unflagged verifier-pass rate (guarded − baseline). Metrics and success definition: success = verifier returns valid=true and automated_flag == FALSE. Models and tools: declared model = gpt-5-mini (as recorded in model_configuration.json). Validator used: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator semantics: full_intent_constraint_validation). Execution adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Max model calls budgeted per pair: one shared initial generation plus up to one repair call for guarded; the run used 301 model calls in total. Sampling and exclusion: pilot (n=60) used only for power calibration; main confirmatory run used 300 analyzable pairs. Exclusion rules: pairs excluded only if both condition calls failed due to infrastructure outage; none met that criterion. Analysis plan: primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar-equivalent with paired bootstrap CI), with pre-specified sensitivity analyses.
sections.results: Execution summary: 600 total episodes completed (300 pairs × 2 conditions); model_calls_used=301; repair stage invoked 1 time (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1). Primary outcome contingency: both pass = 299 pairs; guarded-only pass = 1; baseline-only pass = 0; both fail = 0. Observed rates: baseline success = 299/300 = 0.9967; guarded success = 300/300 = 1.0000. Confirmatory inferential output (paired_binary_analysis_v1): absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap_seed=1729, B=10000). Missingness/exclusions: none. Contamination/negative control: deterministic contamination checks were applied per preregistration; no negative-control anomalies were triggered in the main run. Repair analysis: a single guarded episode required the configured single automated repair; that repair produced a verified pass in guarded but the baseline corresponding pass had failed (the single discordant case).
sections.discussion: Interpretation: In this synthetic benchmark and with the chosen model+validator, baseline single‑shot LLM generation already produced near‑perfect verifier passes, leaving limited headroom for the guarded pipeline to demonstrate a large absolute improvement. The observed absolute improvement (0.33 percentage points) is minimal and statistically non‑significant under the preregistered test due to extreme ceiling performance and very low discordance. Practical implication: when a competent LLM and well‑crafted prompt produce near‑correct proposals, a verifier may still be operationally valuable for deterministic flagging, audit logging, and safety envelopes, but the measurable marginal pass rate increase can be small in benign synthetic tasks. Sources of the ceiling effect: (a) synthetic task generator sampled workflows that were solvable by the model given the prompt constraints; (b) single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) limits generality; (c) verifier coverage was aligned to the synthetic semantics (deterministic validator may match the task generator closely). The single discordant case demonstrates that verifier+repair can rescue rare generation failures, but effect size will depend on base model quality and task difficulty. Exploratory items: failure-mode taxonomy counts were trivial in this run (virtually zero violations), so no stable subgroup conclusions could be drawn. Future work should (i) test harder, more diverse, and real-world configuration corpora; (ii) evaluate multiple LLM backends and verifier implementations; and (iii) measure operational costs (latency, model calls) and human‑in‑the‑loop thresholds for deployment.
sections.conclusion: We report a preregistered, fully archived paired comparison of a verifier-assisted pipeline versus LLM-only single-shot generation for pre-deployment NetOps changes. On our synthetic benchmark with gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, baseline single-shot generation already achieved near‑perfect verifier pass rates (299/300), producing a negligible paired improvement for the guarded pipeline. This result does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in general; rather, it emphasizes that the verifier's measurable marginal benefit depends strongly on task difficulty, model capability, and validator coverage. We release the full preregistration, execution artifacts, and analysis to enable community follow-up evaluations under more challenging and diverse conditions.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by deterministic task generator; real-world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes.
Single model and verifier: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer verifiers.
Ceiling effect: baseline single-shot performance was near 100%, producing limited discordance and low power to detect small absolute improvements.
Operational deployment not evaluated: latency, cost, operator workflows, and human‑in‑the‑loop thresholds were outside the confirmatory scope and require further study.
